content:
Wow. Samsung had a seven-year head start in the foldable market, and Apple has always held the philosophy of 'only shipping something when it can do it better than anyone else' — and the iPhone Duo delivers, spectacularly!

It's clear Apple has thought through every detail of what a folding iPhone should be, and has fully exploited everything this form factor makes possible…

First, there's the fundamentals. Earlier reports said Apple waited until the tech was mature enough to make the crease almost entirely disappear, and to ensure the hinge would be durable enough to withstand countless folds. The latter remains to be proven over time, but the hinge alone shows significant engineering effort.

Then there's the under-display selfie camera — perfectly visible when needed, nearly invisible when not.

Apple also carefully considered the various ways you'd hold and rest the device, and how software could best take advantage of those positions.

I can't remember who first said it, but I find it perfectly apt: great design is when something no one else thought of suddenly seems obvious in hindsight. The original iPhone was a perfect example. Other smartphones at the time still had physical keyboards and required a stylus; the iPhone simply used your finger, with the keyboard only appearing when you needed it. With hindsight, of course a smartphone should work that way.

*Yes, the Duo supports Apple Pencil, but it's not required.

For me, the Duo keynote was packed with moments like this. Why do I have to select a subject in a photo first, then copy and paste it into another app, when I could just drag it directly from the original photo? In hindsight, it seems obvious.

Replacing the selfie timer with 'wait until everyone stops moving, then automatically take the photo.' Also obvious!

The most-liked comment from Jordan

I think Apple's marketing and visuals are as stellar as always. My first reaction is usually: wow, that's so cool, I want it! Then reality kicks in — especially with this one, the £2,000 price tag really kills the buzz, and with supply constraints you'll probably have to order now and not get one until early 2027… every model has gone up in price, even refurbs, and while that's now standard practice, it really takes the shine off the whole thing… I used to tell people to treat phone upgrades like buying a new car — get one and use it for years; that advice feels even more apt now, because phones are nearly as expensive as cars!

There are also some UI features that serve no practical purpose but look beautiful, like the blur effect when you fold the device.

I could go on and on, but ultimately, I had already set the bar incredibly high for this device, and I was still genuinely blown away by how good it is. I'm British; when a Brit says "wow," it's usually sarcastic — but this time I mean it, with zero irony.

This isn't even the right device for me. For my use, an iPhone is roughly 50% ultra-thin camera, 49% pocket computer, and 1% phone. An iPhone 18 Pro Max would suit me far better. But I have an intense case of 'tech lust' for the iPhone Duo.

This brings me back to the 'slightly worst side of Apple' mentioned in the headline. Apple is exceptionally good at producing product videos that make you feel like you could reach through the screen and touch the item. Apple can generate intense desire for products we absolutely shouldn't be buying. I'm not the target customer for the iPhone Duo, but I genuinely, absolutely, unequivocally want one. How about you?
